question: How much sparse Boolean computation can a neural network perform when inputs, intermediate features, and outputs are all linearly represented in superposition?

key_findings.claim: The paper formalizes computation in superposition with epsilon-linear representation, a stronger requirement than probe separability that bounds decoding error for every feature.
key_findings.evidence: Sparse binary variables are encoded into a lower-dimensional activation, and a linear readout must recover each coordinate within prescribed error; this creates an explicit interface for composing computations rather than merely detecting features post hoc.

key_findings.claim: A shallow network can compute all pairwise ANDs of sparse features with subquadratic hidden width, including when inputs are already superposed.
key_findings.evidence: The universal-AND construction replaces the naive one-neuron-per-pair O(m^2) design; the basis-aligned case has polylogarithmic-width dependence under sparsity, while Theorem 2 gives approximately square-root-in-m width for superposed inputs at fixed error factors.

key_findings.claim: Randomly initialized MLP features can already linearly represent the universal-AND outputs, so successful probes need not imply learned or causally used computation.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3 establishes linear representation of U-AND by a random MLP under the stated sparse distribution, yielding polynomially many pairwise features in a substantially smaller hidden space and motivating the paper's warning about probe evidence.

key_findings.claim: Low-depth sparse Boolean circuits can be compressed layerwise, but stable deep composition requires explicit error correction and retains unfavorable depth dependence.
key_findings.evidence: The shallow reduction simulates bounded-depth sparse circuits with width exponential in circuit depth; the deep construction alternates universal-AND and error-correction stages, achieving the stated roughly m^(2/3)s^2 width scaling while accumulating layers with circuit depth.

method.core_idea: Model neural computation as sparse Boolean features encoded and decoded linearly in an activation space, then construct compressed networks for universal pairwise conjunction and circuit simulation.
method.mechanism: Use random or structured embeddings, thresholded nonlinear units, sparse-distribution concentration bounds, and periodic error-correction maps so that many Boolean variables and intermediate gates can share fewer neurons while remaining linearly readable.
assumptions: Features and relevant intermediate computations are binary and sparsely active.
Approximate linear decodability is the right operational definition of representation.
Random-feature concentration regimes and asymptotic widths describe neural-network-scale behavior.
Boolean circuits are an informative abstraction of computations performed by trained continuous networks.

techniques.role: Makes superposed features approximately recoverable through bounded-error linear readouts.
Computes every pairwise conjunction without allocating one unit to every pair.
Shows untrained nonlinear features can make many computed quantities probe-readable.
Refreshes noisy intermediate encodings so deeper sparse circuits can be composed.

evaluations.metric: Hidden width required to linearly represent all pairwise AND outputs
evaluations.result: Constructive theorem reduces width from naive quadratic dependence to polylogarithmic dependence under the paper's sparsity and error parameters
evaluations.baseline: One hidden unit for each of O(m^2) feature pairs

evaluations.result: Theorem 2 gives approximately O(sqrt(m)/epsilon^2) dependence, with additional sparsity/log factors specified in the theorem
Theorem 3 and its corollary allow polynomially more readable pair features than hidden dimensions in the stated asymptotic regime
evaluations.baseline: Interpreting linear-probe success as evidence of trained computation

evaluations.metric: Width and depth of a superposed simulator
evaluations.result: Shallow simulation is exponential in circuit depth; alternating computation and correction gives a deeper construction with about m^(2/3)s^2 width

limitations: The analysis is restricted to sparse binary variables and Boolean circuit operations.
Epsilon-linear representation is a chosen formal criterion and may not match causal use by a downstream network.
Results are constructive and asymptotic rather than measurements of trained real-world networks.
Several bounds hide logarithmic, sparsity, or error factors that matter at finite scale.
Depth remains costly: the shallow construction is exponential in circuit depth and the stable construction inserts correction layers.
failure_modes: Dense coactivation destroys the concentration and low-interference benefits of sparse superposition.
Continuous or high-precision intermediate values may require much greater width than Boolean gates.
A linearly decodable feature can be epiphenomenal rather than causally consumed by later layers.
Distribution shift in feature sparsity can invalidate decoding-error guarantees.
reusable_insights: Ask whether a decoded feature is causally used, because random nonlinear features can support surprisingly strong probes.
Model error correction as part of any theory claiming deep computation in superposition.
Report finite-scale constants and sparsity ranges before treating asymptotic compression as practical capacity.
open_questions: Do trained transformers implement anything close to the universal-AND and error-correction constructions?
Can the theory extend to continuous features, attention, and distribution-dependent causal interventions?
What empirical statistic distinguishes incidental linear decodability from functional superposed computation?

competitive_landscape.title: Toy Models of Superposition
competitive_landscape.difference: Toy Models studies why learned representations pack sparse features into fewer dimensions; the reviewed work constructs computations whose inputs, intermediates, and outputs remain in such compressed representations.

competitive_landscape.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Cunningham et al. learn sparse dictionaries from language-model activations and test interpretability; the reviewed paper gives theoretical Boolean constructions and warns that decodability alone may not demonstrate functional use.

competitive_landscape.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: End-to-end sparse dictionary learning optimizes features to preserve model outputs, addressing functional importance empirically; the reviewed theory explains why ordinary reconstruction or probe access can overstate computational evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: The Persian Rug: solving toy models of superposition using large-scale symmetries
competitive_landscape.difference: The Persian Rug solves representation geometry in toy autoencoders using symmetry; the reviewed work focuses on the capacity to transform sparse superposed features through Boolean computation.

novelty_assessment: The paper advances superposition theory from static representation to explicit computation, with universal-AND and error-corrected circuit constructions and a sharp interpretability warning about probes. Its novelty is mathematical rather than empirical: it does not show that trained modern networks use these constructions or that its Boolean sparsity assumptions hold in practice.
reviewer_notes: Read all definitions and main constructions, the random-MLP result, circuit simulations, interpretability discussion, and proof appendices needed to check scope. Direct primary arXiv records on representation, sparse dictionaries, and later analytic superposition were checked on 2026-08-23.
